title: Vibrations & Sound
keyIdea: Every sound is made by something vibrating: moving back and forth very fast. A plucked rubber band, a drum skin, a guitar string and the voice box in your throat all vibrate when they make a sound. When the vibrating stops, the sound stops. It works the other way too: sound travels through the air and can make other things vibrate, like a drum skin that throws rice up when you shout close to it. Some vibrations are too fast and small to see, but you can feel them or show them with water.
familyTip: Stretch a rubber band over an open box or tub and pluck it. Watch it blur, then touch it to stop the sound. Next, put a hand on your throat and hum, then stop: feel the buzz come and go. Last, stretch cling film over a bowl, sprinkle on some rice and bang a pan lid close by.

visual.caption: What vibrates to make the sound? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card then a box.

bins: This part does not make the sound
items: The voice box in your throat

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pluck a band, stop it with a finger, find what vibrates, shout at a drum with rice on it, and dip a humming tuning fork in water.

kid: Pluck a rubber band. It moves back and forth very fast. This is called a vibration. The vibration makes the sound.
Hold the band still. The sound stops. No vibration means no sound.
Lots of things vibrate to make sound. A drum skin shakes when you hit it. A guitar string shakes when you pluck it. When you hum, your voice box shakes. Put a hand on your throat and feel it buzz.

Sound can make things vibrate too. Put rice on a drum and shout close by. The sound makes the drum skin shake, and the rice jumps. Some things shake too fast to see. A humming fork in water makes a splash.
adult: Ages 6 to 9. In England, Year 4 science asks children to find out how sounds are made, and to link them to something vibrating. Children also learn that the vibrations travel through the air to the ear. In the US, NGSS 1-PS4-1 says vibrating things can make sound and sound can make things vibrate. Key words: sound, vibrate, vibration, source, travel, voice box.

Common mistakes: thinking the thing that hits makes the sound (the drumstick, not the drum skin); thinking the hole in a guitar makes the sound; thinking a sound goes on after the source stops vibrating; thinking a vibration must be big enough to see; and saying your breath made the rice jump. A careful test: hold a card in front of your mouth, or bang a pan lid instead. The rice still jumps.

This lesson is about where sound comes from and what it can do. Loud and quiet (how hard you hit) and high and low (how fast it vibrates) are other lessons. So the lab only asks: is it vibrating or not?

In the lab your child plucks a band and sees it blur, then touches it to stop the sound. They tap the part that vibrates on a drum, a guitar and a singer. They move a singer near or far from a drum with rice on it, then shout. Last, they tap a tuning fork on a rubber block and dip it in water.

practice.prompt: You pluck a rubber band. What makes the sound?
choices: The band moving back and forth fast
The air in the room getting warm
practice.hint: Watch the band after you let go. What is it doing?
practice.explain: The band vibrates: it moves back and forth very fast. That vibration makes the sound.

practice.prompt: A band shakes back and forth {n} times each second for {s} seconds. How many shakes is that?
practice.hint: It does {n} shakes in each second. Add {n} for every second.
practice.explain: {n} shakes each second for {s} seconds is {n} × {s} = {=n*s} shakes. Vibrations are fast!

practice.prompt: A bell is ringing. You hold it tight with your hand. What happens?
practice.hint: Your hand stops the bell moving.
practice.explain: Your hand stops the bell vibrating. No vibration means no sound.

practice.prompt: There are {r} grains of rice on a drum. You shout close by and {j} of them jump. How many stay still?
practice.hint: Take the grains that jumped away from all the grains.
practice.explain: {r} take away {j} is {=r-j}. The sound made the skin vibrate and threw the other grains up.

practice.prompt: When you hum, which part of you vibrates to make the sound?
choices: Your voice box in your throat
practice.hint: Put your hand on your throat and hum. Where do you feel a buzz?
practice.explain: The voice box in your throat vibrates. You feel it as a buzz under your hand.

choices: Move back and forth very fast
pool.hint: Think of a plucked rubber band.
pool.explain: To vibrate is to move back and forth very fast, again and again.

pool.prompt: You hit a drum with a stick. What vibrates to make the sound?
pool.hint: The stick hits something. What shakes after the hit?
pool.explain: The stick hits the skin, then the skin vibrates. That vibration makes the sound.

pool.prompt: Which part of a guitar vibrates to make the sound?
pool.hint: Which part do you pluck with your fingers?
pool.explain: You pluck the strings and they vibrate. The hole only lets the sound out.

pool.prompt: Rice sits on a drum. You shout close to it and the rice jumps. Why?
choices: The sound makes the drum skin vibrate
pool.explain: The sound travels through the air and makes the skin vibrate. The skin throws the rice up. Your breath is too far away to move it.

pool.prompt: A tuning fork hums but looks still. You dip it in water. What happens?
pool.hint: It is humming, so is it vibrating?
pool.explain: The fork vibrates too fast to see. In water, the fast shaking throws water up in a splash.

pool.prompt: You pluck {a} bands. Then you touch {b} of them to stop them. How many bands still make a sound?
pool.hint: A band you touch stops vibrating, so it stops making sound.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}. Only the bands still vibrating make a sound.

pool.prompt: A drum stops vibrating. What happens to the sound?
pool.hint: Sound is only made while something is vibrating.
pool.explain: The sound stops. Sound is only made while something is vibrating.

pool.prompt: You stand far away and shout at the drum. The rice only wobbles. Why?
choices: The sound is weaker when it gets there
The rice is too heavy to ever move
pool.hint: What happened when you moved closer?
pool.explain: Sound spreads out as it travels, so it is weaker far away. Move closer and the skin vibrates more.

pool.prompt: A drum skin vibrates {n} times each second. How many times does it vibrate in {s} seconds?
pool.hint: Add {n} for each second, or work out {n} × {s}.
pool.explain: {n} times each second for {s} seconds is {n} × {s} = {=n*s} vibrations. That is too fast to count by eye.
